## **User description** ## What changed The site is now one page instead of three. The home page holds the photo, name and job title, contacts, bio and the whole CV. The old About, Résumé and Work pages are removed. Their addresses, with or without `.html` or a trailing slash, redirect to the home page. A 404 page is added. ### The CV - `cv.yaml` holds the CV, in RenderCV's format. - Logan's name, job title, bio, email, website, location, profiles and other contacts are typed in `cv.yaml` only. The build copies them into a settings file for Jekyll, `_config.cv.yml`, made fresh each time and not kept in the repo. The site needs only the name and website; whatever else `cv.yaml` leaves out, the pages leave out too. - `cv.yaml` fills every part of RenderCV's template: the header in the template's order, `design`, `locale` and `settings`. Its 31 contacts are 8 profiles and 23 custom connections, including Signal and WhatsApp, which the contact line, `logan.vcf` and `security.txt` read from there, each only when `cv.yaml` lists it. The photo is a crop of the sand dunes portrait, `images/cv-photo.jpg`. The PDF shows the photo and all 31 contacts; the home page's copy of the CV comes from RenderCV's Markdown template, which has no photo and lists only the 8 profiles. - The CV's text has no hand formatting: no bold or italics, only links, quotes and middle dots. - The name's two parts for `logan.vcf` are in `_config.yml`, since `cv.yaml` has no place for them. - The build runs RenderCV 2.8. Its HTML goes on the home page and its PDF at `/cv.pdf`. RenderCV's whole output folder is also published, at `/rendercv_output/`. - `markdown/` holds copies of RenderCV's own Markdown templates. They're changed only to set the heading levels, so the page has one `h1`. ### Look - The layout sits on a graph-paper grid of squares, each one line of text tall. - Light and dark themes follow the visitor's system setting. A moon/sun switch changes the theme, and the choice lasts for the browser session. - Ten colors are set in `_config.yml`. - Three typefaces are served from the site with their licenses, and set by tag: - Gelasio (serif) for body text and lists - DejaVu Sans for the header and headings - Cousine (mono) for the contacts, the photo caption and the footer's small print ### Home page - Eleven Idaho photos rotate every 7 seconds, in a random order for each visit. Each has alt text and its place name as the caption. The rotation stops for visitors who ask for reduced motion. - Contacts: email, Signal and WhatsApp. - The footer has a fire animation in the site's colors, after Filipe Deschamps's doom-fire-algorithm (MIT). It pauses while the footer is off screen, and doesn't run for reduced motion. ### Describing the site and Logan to software - Jekyll's SEO plugin adds the title, description and link-preview tags. It also adds a search-engine block describing a person, with the 31 contacts from `cv.yaml`. `rel="me"` links point to the same 31. - Other machine-readable pieces: - contact-card (h-card) labels on the home page - `logan.vcf` - `humans.txt` - `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` - `.well-known/webfinger` and `.well-known/security.txt` - `site.webmanifest` - a sitemap and `robots.txt`. `robots.txt` has a `Content-Signal` line: search and AI answers yes, AI training no - `trust.txt` (JournalList's format), at `/trust.txt` and `/.well-known/trust.txt`: the current memberships from `cv.yaml`, the same 31 accounts, the contacts, and `datatrainingallowed=no` - `.well-known/tdmrep.json`, which reserves text-and-data-mining rights, and `.well-known/gpc.json`, which says the site honors Global Privacy Control - A `fediverse:creator` tag credits Logan on Mastodon's link previews. It works once the account's server runs Mastodon 4.3 or later and the domain is added under Author attribution there; syringa.social runs 4.2.19. ### Build and repo - The Pages workflow: 1. renders the CV 2. copies the site's facts from `cv.yaml` for Jekyll 3. on the daily run, checks whether the CV's text changed, through an edit or a date rolling over, and publishes only if it did 4. draws the favicon and app icons from `favicon.svg` 5. builds the site with Jekyll, through the github-pages gem: the same Jekyll and plugin versions GitHub Pages uses 6. checks, with html-proofer, that the site's own links, images, scripts and link-preview images exist (links to other sites aren't checked) 7. runs pa11y-ci at WCAG AAA on the home page, in both themes, and on the 404 page - Python packages are pinned in `.github/requirements.txt` and Ruby gems in `Gemfile.lock`. Dependabot watches both, plus the test tools and the workflow's actions. - `_config.yml` sets the site's base address, so the build doesn't depend on GitHub's API for it. - The TTF fonts in `fonts/` are for the PDF only and aren't published; the site serves the WOFF2 files. - Adds CODEOWNERS, FUNDING, issue templates, SECURITY.md and a PR template. - Removes `CNAME`, which GitHub ignores when Pages builds from Actions. - Removes `config.js`. Its code now lives in `theme.js` and `hero.js`. ### Between visits The repo assumes a person looks in only now and then. - Dependabot's minor and patch updates merge themselves once the build and tests pass on their pull request. Only the commit the build tested can merge. Major updates, updates that change the workflow, and pull requests with any commit not by Dependabot wait for a person. - Each daily run re-enables itself. GitHub switches off a public repository's scheduled runs after 60 days without activity. That re-enabling resets the count comes from community keepalive workflows; GitHub's docs don't say. - Runs wait their turn in order (`queue: max`), so a daily run can't replace a waiting push and leave its changes unpublished. - A failed daily run opens an issue, "The daily site build failed", assigned to loganfinney27. If that issue is already open, it adds a comment instead. - After each publish, the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine is asked to save the home page and the pages it links to (Save Page Now), skipping any saved in the last 30 days. It needs a free archive.org account's keys as the secrets `ARCHIVE_ORG_ACCESS_KEY` and `ARCHIVE_ORG_SECRET_KEY`, and does nothing without them. If the archive can't take the request, the run shows a warning, not a failure. - `README.md` says what to do on a visit: how to change the CV, what runs by itself, what waits, how to switch on the Wayback Machine copies, and how to switch the daily check back on if GitHub ever turns it off. ### Checks - Each change was checked by building the site before and after, comparing screenshots at 1280 and 390 px, and running pa11y-ci. - The move to reading `cv.yaml` was checked by comparing every built file with the previous build. All 87 are identical. - Moving the contacts into `cv.yaml` was checked by building before and after: the contact line, `logan.vcf`, `security.txt` and `humans.txt` are unchanged, and a parse of `cv.yaml` shows the CV's text changed only by the removed `*` marks. A test build without Signal, WhatsApp or the email leaves no empty rows or lines. - The GitHub build passes on `9f5c88e`. - A manual run on the branch re-enabled the daily run with GitHub's own token. - The merge decision was tested locally against 14 cases. Patch and minor updates merge. These wait: a major update, a mix, no update type, a workflow change, a commit by someone else (including one past the first 30 commits), and a commit with no GitHub account. If the pull request moves on while the build runs, the merge is refused. If GitHub fails to answer any lookup, the step stops and nothing merges. - The link check passes on GitHub's build, and catches a missing stylesheet, a missing link-preview image and a link to a missing part of a page in a copy broken on purpose. - The archive job was tested locally against a stand-in for the archive: no keys, a request taken and saved, a busy or refused request, a failed save, and a save still running after 2 minutes. It has yet to run against the real archive; it will on the first publish after the keys are added. - The merge job and the failure issue have yet to run for real. They will on the first Dependabot pull request and the first failed daily run. If the main branch's rules stop the workflow from merging, the update simply waits for a person. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_014e9aGs3SxNfCer3Nmunb6e ___ ## **CodeAnt-AI Description** **Create a print-inspired journalist portfolio with a complete on-page CV** ### What Changed - Gives the site a ruled, graph-paper look with light and dark themes. - Adds a rotating gallery of captioned Idaho photos, alongside an introduction and email, Signal, and WhatsApp links. - Brings experience, awards, education, memberships, and portfolio credits together in a CV on the homepage; former About, Resume, and Work addresses lead there. ### Impact `✅ Resume and portfolio details together on one page` `✅ Captions identify the featured Idaho scenes` `✅ Theme choice retained during a browsing session`
💡 Usage Guide ### Checking Your Pull Request Every time you make a pull request, our system automatically looks through it. items.title: Rewrite core engine in Go; add CLI, CI pipeline, and contract testing
items.body:
Telescope started as a fully TypeScript/Bun-based OpenAPI linter and VS Code extension (`packages/telescope-server/`). As the feature set grew — more rules, cross-file `$ref` resolution, multi-version schema validation — the TypeScript implementation hit a performance ceiling. This PR replaces the entire TypeScript server with a Go core, restructures the repository from `packages/` to a flat layout, and adds a full CLI, CI pipeline, GitHub Action, and contract testing capability.

The Go core is built on a stack of purpose-built libraries: **Navigator** (OpenAPI parsing and indexing), **Barrelman** (shared rule library with 88 built-in rules), **Barometer** (contract testing), and **Gossip** (LSP framework). Telescope is the experience layer — editor, CLI, CI — that ties them together.

**Scope**: 93 commits, 849 files changed, +134k / -61k lines.

---

## Architecture

| | **main** (TypeScript) | **This PR** (Go) |
|---|---|---|
| **Server** | `packages/telescope-server/` (Bun/TS) | `server/` (Go) |
| **Client** | `packages/telescope-client/` | `client/` (promoted to root) |
| **Test fixtures** | `packages/test-files/` | `test-files/` (promoted to root) |
| **Workspace layout** | pnpm workspaces in `packages/` | Flat: `server/`, `client/`, `test-files/` |
| **Built-in rules** | 52 (TypeScript) | 88 (54 core + 32 OWASP + 2 syntax checks) |
| **Custom rules** | TS rules loaded in-process | TS rules via compiled Bun sidecar binary |
| **YAML declarative rules** | N/A | JSONPath (Spectral-style) or tree-sitter pattern rules |
| **Spectral rulesets** | Embedded in server process | Via Bun sidecar + native Spectral engine mapping |
| **Schema validation** | Zod + AJV (in-process) | Navigator-backed structural validation |
| **Parsing** | Spectral parsers (JS) | Tree-sitter (incremental, Go bindings) |
| **Child LSPs** | N/A | yaml-language-server + vscode-json-language-server |
| **CLI** | N/A | `telescope lint`, `ci`, `validate`, `serve`, `bundle`, `contract test` |
| **CI / GitHub Action** | N/A | `action.yml` composite action + `telescope ci` command |
| **Contract testing** | N/A | Barometer integration (CLI + VS Code command) |
| **Go library SDK** | N/A | `server/sdk/` — `LintFiles()`, `LintContent()`, `Workspace` API |

---

## Server reliability improvements

### Graceful shutdown
- `NewServer()` returns a cleanup function that stops child LSPs, Bun sidecar, and cleans temp files
- All background goroutines use a cancellable context (`bgCtx`) instead of `context.Background()`
- `serve.go` calls `defer cleanup()` after `gossip.Serve()` returns

### Error handling
- `NewGraphBridge()` returns error instead of `panic()` — server degrades gracefully if graph pipeline fails
- `clientForURI()` race condition fixed — mutex held through return via `defer m.mu.Unlock()`

### Client crash recovery
- `onDidChangeState` handler detects when server process stops unexpectedly
- `scheduleRestart()` implements exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s) up to 5 attempts
- After max attempts, shows error message directing user to manual restart command

### Build pipeline
- Release binary now includes version via `-ldflags -X lsp.Version=<pkg_version>`
- GitHub Action temp file cleaned up via `trap 'rm -f "$err_file"' EXIT`

---

## E2E test suite

33 test files with 94 test cases covering all LSP features across single-root, multi-root, and sidecar workspaces. The suite runs on Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows in CI with smoke mode for PRs and full mode on main.

### Test architecture
- **Event-based synchronization** — `waitForDiagnostics`, `waitForProviders`, `waitForDocumentAnalyzed`, `waitForCrossFileReady` replace hard-coded delays
- **Fixture-pinned assertions** — tests assert exact schema names, diagnostic codes, hover content structure, and token types against `rich-api.yaml`
- **Mocha retries** (`TELESCOPE_E2E_RETRIES=1`) in CI for eventually-consistent operations
- **Platform-aware timeouts** — Windows CI gets longer timeouts for code lens polling
- **Graceful sidecar handling** — tests skip on platforms where Bun sidecar isn't available

### Coverage by feature

| Feature | Tests | What's validated |
|---------|-------|------------------|
| Activation & sessions | 4 | Extension activates, test API exposed, sessions start, restart recovery |
| Diagnostics | 10 | Specific codes (oas3-schema, unresolved-ref, duplicate-opid), severity levels, zero errors on valid specs |
| Hover | 7 | Schema properties (email, id), operationId shows GET /users, tag shows description, negative case |
| Completion | 3 | All 4 schema names (User, CreateUserRequest, Pet, Error), HTTP method completions |
| Definition | 5 | Local and cross-file $ref resolution, hover on target, document symbols, find references |
| Code actions | 3 | Quickfix/suppress/documentation actions, action titles validated |
| Code lens | 3 | Reference count pattern, health score format, OpenAPI version header |
| Document highlight | 2 | Write kind for definitions, Read kind for usages, count >= 5 for User schema |
| Semantic tokens | 2 | Token types 8 (variable/$ref), 10 (function/operationId), 11 (method/HTTP) |
| Inlay hints | 2 | Type kind hints with resolved type labels, padding |
| Folding ranges | 2 | Range count >= 10, ranges cover document regions |
| Symbols | 4 | Path names (/users, /pets), schema names (User, Pet), workspace symbol search |
| Rename | 3 | Tag rename, non-renameable position, cross-file schema rename |
| Document links | 2 | $ref links with targets, cross-file link resolution |
| Type definition | 2 | $ref resolves to schema definition, empty for non-ref position |
| Call hierarchy | 3 | Prepare on schema, incoming calls (4+ $ref usages), outgoing calls (Pet→User) |
| Selection range | 2 | Property→schema expansion chain, operation→path expansion |
| Formatting | 1 | JSON pretty-print with newlines (when child LSP available) |
| Language IDs | 4 | openapi-yaml, openapi-json, plain yaml, reclassification on edit |
| Commands | 3 | generateResponseSkeletons, bundlePreview (sortTags/sortPaths skipped — tested in Go) |
| File sync | 3 | Create/change/remove diagnostics, cross-file diagnostic propagation |
| Multi-root | 4 | Per-folder sessions, diagnostics isolation, delta isolation, per-folder providers |
| Sidecar | 11 | Custom rules, generic rules, lifecycle, multi-file refs, OpenAPI rules, schema fixtures |
| No bulk open | 1 | Startup scan doesn't open all files |

### CI pipeline

| Step | Timeout | Details |
|------|---------|---------|
| Single-root | 15 min | 33 test files (excludes sidecar/multi-root) |
| Multi-root | 20 min | 2 test files (activation + multi-root) |
| Sidecar | 15 min | 8 test files (activation + 7 sidecar) |
| Job overall | 45 min | Prevents runaway jobs |
| Mocha retries | 1 | Retries failed tests once in CI |

---

## CI status

| Job | Ubuntu | macOS | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| Go build/test/vet | :white_check_mark: | :white_check_mark: | :white_check_mark: |
| TypeScript build | :white_check_mark: | — | — |
| Benchmarks | :white_check_mark: | — | — |
| E2E single-root | :white_check_mark: | :white_check_mark: | :white_check_mark: |
| E2E multi-root | :white_check_mark: | :white_check_mark: | :white_check_mark: |
| E2E sidecar | :white_check_mark: | :white_check_mark: | :white_check_mark: (skips custom rule tests — Bun sidecar doesn't start on Windows) |
| Telescope self-lint | :white_check_mark: | — | — |

---

## Breaking changes

- **Server runtime** — Go binary replaces the Node.js/Bun server process
- **`packages/` directory removed** — `client/` and `test-files/` are at repo root
- **Config format** — `.telescope.yaml` fields updated (see `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`)
- **Built-in rule IDs** — rule set expanded from 52 to 88; some rule IDs may have changed
- **Build requirements** — Go 1.25+ required for the server, Node.js for the VS Code extension build, Bun for the custom rule sidecar binary

Custom TypeScript rules using `defineRule()` / `defineGenericRule()` from the `@sailpoint-oss/telescope` SDK continue to work via the Bun sidecar.

---

## Documentation

Fully rewritten to reflect the new architecture:

- **Rewritten**: `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`
- **New**: `docs/RULES.md` (88-rule reference), `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`, `docs/CUSTOM-RULES.md`, `docs/LSP-FEATURES.md`, `docs/CODEBASE-BREAKDOWN.md`, `docs/CI.md`, `docs/SDK.md`, `docs/PUBLISHING.md`

---

## Test plan

- [x] `cd server && go build ./...` — compiles on Linux, macOS, Windows
- [x] `cd server && go vet ./...` — passes on all platforms
- [x] `cd server && go test -race ./... -timeout 10m` — all tests pass on all platforms
- [x] `pnpm --filter ./client run build` — client extension builds
- [x] `pnpm --filter ./client run typecheck` — no type errors
- [x] `pnpm --filter telescope run test` — 384 unit tests pass
- [x] E2E single-root: 74 passing on all platforms
- [x] E2E multi-root: passing on all platforms
- [x] E2E sidecar: passing on Ubuntu/macOS, gracefully skipped on Windows
- [x] Benchmarks complete and comparison posted
- [x] Telescope self-lint passes on `test-files/`

milestone.title: Verified records, dataset assembly, and admission
milestone.description: Assemble validated records into new reproducible datasets with source replay, canonical identity, deduplication, quality gates, rights evidence, train/eval separation, and fail-closed export. Require inspectable manifests and retained/rejected accounting. Replaces the Factory v0.2.0 version bucket: v0.2.0/v0.3.0 work advanced non-sequentially, so track actual capability outcomes while preserving completed work. Hosted frontier outputs remain research-only; training admission requires explicit project and provider permission plus verified evidence.

items.body:
Generates fresh neuromorphic records and carries authenticated measurements through validation, dataset assembly, and local export. Five reference families cover encoder equivalence, neuron counterfactuals, synaptic delays, neuromodulator credit assignment, and temporal memory.

The optional Rust backend now uses actual locked crates.io dependencies `axon-encoder = 0.4.0` and `neuromod = 0.6.0`. `oracle_generate.py --backend rust --oracle-rust-bin PATH` selects versioned crate-native encoder and neuron profiles. Reference remains the default and ignores ambient runtime commands. Unsupported families/configurations and missing executables fail explicitly, without fallback or automatic compilation.

- `axon-stream-v1` calls deterministic streaming rate/delta encoders and retains full events, bounded previews, and explicitly adapter-derived reconstruction/RMSE.
- `neuromod-lif-v1` calls the crate's standalone LIF integration and firing methods for threshold, decay, and input-intensity interventions, retaining spikes and pre-reset voltage traces. It does not claim the reference model's adaptation/refractory dynamics.
- Records bind profiles/configuration, released crate revisions, dependency lock, adapter source hash, build-time Git base revision, and executable SHA-256. The independent reviewed source seal includes Rust manifests, lockfile, build script, and production modules.
- Validation, compose, and export accept explicit `--oracle-rust-bin PATH` authority to freshly replay native records. Metadata cannot select or execute a command; no cached CLI report grants admission. Other external runtime records remain ineligible without supported replay authority.
- Assembly preserves original source text and coordinates. Explicit eligible-training selection authenticates excluded evidence too, and export replays source-to-output decisions before writing local splits.

Validation at published commit `ec9f23d7`: a clean public-CLI run with seed `20260918` generated 16 new records across both native families. All 16 were accepted and reproduced with zero invalid records, all 16 were assembled, and local export produced 14 train / 2 evaluation rows. Original record bytes and both retained payload files were verified through source, curated output, and export. The reference fixture was regenerated through its diagnostic replay helper; all 20 scenarios and measured results remained identical.

Local locked Rust build, formatting, Clippy, six Rust tests, 593 oracle Python tests, and 33 compatibility/import/facade tests passed. Promotion coverage passed after fixing a test that assumed all deadline-bound fixture records would survive. Regression tests also cover rehashed identity/measurement tampering, missing executables, strict profiles, CRLF checkout preservation, and authenticated non-UTF-8 payload rejection. CI builds the locked executable and runs native end-to-end tests on Python 3.14.

Usage and limitations: [Rust backend guide](https://github.com/rmems/synthetic-factory/blob/main/docs/oracle-rust-backend.md).

Integrated main through append-only merges; no public history rewrite of pre-push commits. Final head `dc23e418` passed every applicable gate before merge: unittest (Python 3.14, 28m), operator smoke + fixture census, qlty check + fmt, Qodana, CodeScene, Codacy, SonarCloud, CodeRabbit, and codecov/patch. The quality-gate findings across oracle, curation, simulator, export, and Rust modules were paid down by refactoring — including a reviewed-pattern allowlist for schema regexes (S2631), procfs-bound argv identity in the Rust adapter, shared test helpers for the oracle CLI case splits, and sealed-source digest regeneration — with no suppressions and fail-closed integrity preserved.

Squash-merged as `95a75f8b` on 2026-09-19. No remote dataset publication, Spikenaut training, FPGA parity, or model-quality improvement is claimed. Dataset snapshot splits are not independent scientific evaluation.

The follow-up also seals all delegated oracle sources, repairs package-mode generator imports, validates exact staging membership with independent directory cursors, and preserves real admitted fixture membership in promotion assertions. Per-record source verification remains deliberate: replacing it with a mutable-checkout cache would weaken admission unless the whole batch first receives an authenticated immutable source snapshot.

Relates to #77.

items.title: Global TESSERA setup
items.body:
## Global TESSERA setup

Stands up the **global 10-metre embeddings campaign** end to end — everything
needed to produce one embedding per pixel, per year, for the whole land surface
of the planet, and to drive that at production scale.

The globe is divided into 120 map zones (the 60 UTM bands, north and south).
This PR adds the storage that holds all 120, the machinery to prepare each
zone's satellite inputs and run the model over them, and the orchestration that
seeds the store, builds a land mask, and then ingests-and-fills every zone for
every year — restartable, cost-bounded, and safe to cancel. It stays current
with `main` throughout (it carries the recently merged inference-performance
rework and profiling tooling so the campaign runs on the latest inference path).

The older single-region pipeline is **not** replaced or left behind: the two now
share one geometry and one set of pre-flight gates end to end, so a fix to either
is a fix to both. That convergence is described under "One geometry, both
pipelines" below.

It's a large change, so the sections below are organised by component rather
than by file.

## The pieces

### One global store

All 120 zones live in a single versioned store. Each zone is seeded once with a
fixed set of yearly slots (2017–2025) that are never resized afterwards, which
keeps the store's internal bookkeeping cheap even at planetary scale. The
per-pixel results are stored compressed and space-efficiently, and ocean areas
are elided so we don't pay to store empty water.

**Time labels are guaranteed accurate.** Each yearly slot is labelled by its
calendar year and is only ever allowed to hold that exact January–December
window; the covered date range is recorded alongside the data, and the fill
step refuses to write any non-calendar window. So a slot's label always matches
what's actually in it. (The store's README shows the recommended way to open a
zone and read these.)

Zones are identified everywhere by their human name (`"33N"`, `"07S"`) rather
than an opaque code, so store groups, file paths, and progress tags all read
the same way.

### Land mask — the coverage registry *is* the mask

Rather than storing giant per-pixel land/ocean masks, we derive which map tiles
are land directly from the coverage registry the data partner supplies, using
geometry alone (no heavy data reads). This produces small per-zone "which tiles
are live" bitmaps in seconds, and turns what used to be tens of thousands of
reads per fill into a single lookup — saving on the order of millions of
storage requests across a full campaign.

Each zone's mask can be built on demand by the campaign, or generated for every
zone ahead of time by a separate flow that also **validates** them. The check
worth having is placement: it asserts that the mask marks land exactly where the
coverage registry says land is, and nowhere else. A mask with the right amount of
land in the wrong place would otherwise surface hours later as data written to the
wrong ground position, so a green run of that flow — rather than a log line — is
the evidence that every zone's mask is correct before a campaign spends anything.

### Per-zone data ingestion

The satellite inputs for a zone-year (a multi-terabyte "mosaic" of optical and
radar imagery) are prepared on demand by the campaign, reusing the existing
region-ingest engine. Ingestion is **idempotent and crash-safe**: a fingerprint
records what was ingested and under what settings, a half-written or stale
mosaic is detected and rebuilt rather than appended onto, and the "done" marker
is only written after coverage is verified. Because these mosaics are large and
fully re-derivable, they're treated as **transient** — deleted automatically
once the zone's results are committed (a keep-flag retains them for debugging).

### Ingesting only the land

A zone is mostly water. The first real campaign cell exposed that ingestion did
not care: it built its mosaic across a zone's **entire** rectangle regardless of
how much of that rectangle was land, so its cost tracked the zone's size rather
than its content. The cell chosen as the cheapest possible test — the smallest
land zone on Earth in this scheme, four tiles of Pacific islands — became the
most expensive thing the project had run, holding about a terabyte of imagery
across memory and disk to obtain those four tiles, killing its own workers, and
having to be abandoned. Measured across all 112 land zones, roughly **78% of the
campaign's ingestion effort would have gone into mosaicking open ocean.**

Ingestion now reads the land mask first and computes only the parts of the grid
that contain land. It does this in two stages, and the second turned out to
matter more than the first.

**Stage one** covers each row of the grid with one rectangle spanning that row's
land. The strategy was chosen from measurements rather than intuition: whole-row
rectangles land within about 2% of the theoretical best, whereas the obvious
alternative — a single box around all the land — recovers less than half, because
a zone holding scattered islands down its length is barely narrowed by one box.
On that first cell this took 3,706 blocks per band per date down to 4.

**Stage two** merges vertically adjacent rectangles into fewer, taller ones. That
computes some water, which sounds like a step backwards, but the two costs are
nothing alike: area is computed in parallel across the whole fleet, while every
extra rectangle is a separate blocking write the whole fleet waits through. Once
that was measured rather than assumed, the balance was obvious — merging is worth
it almost whenever it is geometrically sane. Every zone now ingests in two to five
rectangles instead of up to a couple of hundred, and on the reference cell it cut
the time per date by **6.2×**, far more than stage one did.

A third, finer stage applies per date: a satellite images only a strip of a wide
zone on any given pass, so each date is narrowed again to the rectangles its own
imagery can actually reach. This cannot change what gets stored — it only skips
work whose result was going to be empty — but it removes both computation and
whole blocking writes from dates that cover little of the zone.

Two properties make this safe rather than merely cheaper. The mosaic still
*declares* the full zone grid, so the checks that validate it against the
authoritative grid are untouched and no consumer sees a different shape — the
storage format is sparse, so the untouched parts cost nothing and read back as
empty. And each date is written as a single atomic transaction covering both the
date's entry and its pixels, so an interrupted run cannot leave a date that looks
ingested but holds nothing, which the deduplication logic would otherwise skip
over permanently.

Two of the 60 UTM bands straddle the international date line, where a bounding
box wraps around from +180° to -180°. Catalog queries for those zones are split
at the line and their results merged, so zones that would otherwise return no
imagery — or an unbounded amount of it — behave like every other zone.

The same work removes two related problems the cell exposed: a zone's worker
fleet is now sized from its land content rather than being a fixed number (a
four-tile zone had been given the same fleet as a dense one), and a cancelled or
crashed ingestion now shuts its cluster down instead of leaving it running.

It ships **switched off** at every layer, so the previous full-extent behaviour is
byte-for-byte unchanged for anyone who does not ask for it. The cropped path has
since been exercised extensively on live cells (see the next section), and turning
it on is the campaign's intended configuration.

### Making ingestion fast enough to actually run

Cropping made a dense zone possible; it did not make it affordable. Ingesting a
dense zone-month went from **not completing at all** to about **185 seconds per
date**, which puts a dense zone-year at roughly 11 hours rather than the ~70 it
would have been uncropped. Getting there took a run of individually small changes,
each worth naming because each removed a different bottleneck:

- **The query is streamed a month at a time.** Asking the satellite catalog for a
  whole year up front means holding every result for the run's duration, and a
  zone-year's worth does not fit alongside the ingestion on one machine. Each
  month is now fetched while the previous one is being ingested, so only two are
  ever held. Each returned record is also stripped to the fields actually used
  before being kept, which cut what the query retains by a further **2.45×**.
- **A date's rectangles are written together.** They used to be computed one after
  another, so a date cost the *sum* of its rectangles rather than the slowest of
  them. Submitting them as one piece of work cut time per date by **1.59×**, and
  the resulting stores are byte-for-byte identical.
- **How much is read at once was separated from how it is stored** — and later
  re-unified, which is worth the honesty: the coarser read blocks cut the
  coordination work an order of magnitude, but they also capped how many machines
  a date could keep busy, and on compact regions that cap cost more than the
  coordination ever did. Measured head-to-head the split was a wash on dense
  zones and **2× slower** on compact ones, so it is gone again; the follow-on
  batching below recovers the coordination relief a better way.
- **Bookkeeping was sharded by time**, so committing one date stops rewriting the
  index for every date before it.

Two things were deliberately left alone: how the mosaic is chunked on disk, which
the GPU stage is tuned around, and the rule that each date commits atomically,
which is what makes an interrupted ingestion safe to retry.

Worth stating plainly for anyone planning follow-on work: **a single date cannot
fill a large fleet by itself.** A date's work only comes in as many independent
pieces as its area has blocks, so past that width extra machines stand idle no
matter how the work is scheduled. The campaign's real multipliers are running
many zones at once and, within a zone, computing several dates together — both of
which it now does.

### Several dates computed as one piece of work

The pieces above make one date cheap; this makes dates stop paying their overheads
one at a time. `batch_dates` groups up to k consecutive kept dates and runs their
loads, masks and writes as **one piece of work landing as one commit** — so the
dates pack the fleet together, one date's slow reads backfill with another's
writes, and the per-date ramp, drain and commit gap are paid once per batch.

One commit per batch is forced, not preferred: every date's append resizes the
store's time axis, so two dates committed separately from the same starting point
collide on that shared bookkeeping even though their pixels never overlap. The
practical consequences are spelled out in the code and docs — a failed batch
commits none of its dates, an interrupted run re-ingests exactly the dates that
never landed, and stores are **byte-for-byte identical** to the one-date-at-a-time
path (pinned by a test whose gate-failing date sits mid-batch). Off by default;
dates that fail the cloud gate never occupy a batch slot.

Two companion guards from the same measurement campaign: date **pipelining**
(prepare the next date while the current one writes) ships behind a flag with a
fleet-width bound above which the flow declines to pipeline rather than quietly
running slower, and the profiling toolkit gained the three queries every one of
these A/Bs was actually judged from — per-date stage timings, their batched
counterpart, and how much preparation the pipeline hid — so the next measurement
starts from tooling rather than ad-hoc log greps.

### Writing results — a simpler assembly engine

The step that assembles per-pixel results into the store was rewritten to write
directly to the storage format using its native fork-and-merge mechanism,
replacing the old Dask-based engine that struggled at this scale. Publishing is
atomic: a reader never sees a half-written year, and re-running a zone cleanly
replaces exactly what that run produced.

### One geometry, both pipelines

The campaign and the single-region pipeline had drifted into two different
storage geometries, and the single-region one was the shape history left rather
than a shape anyone chose. They now use the same one throughout, so every stage
divides evenly into the next and nothing is re-cut in between:

```
4096 px ingest chunk → 2048 px inference tile → 2048 px output shard → 256 px chunk
```

Two things came out of that beyond the tidiness. A pixel's 128 values used to be
split across 32 separate objects on the single-region path, so reading one
pixel's embedding cost 32 reads; it is now one. And because the assembly workers
divide the map on the same pitch as the tiles, each tile is read exactly once
instead of once per band it happened to straddle.

The comparison also turned up three places where the single-region path was
behind the campaign, all now fixed: an unusable worker count and an
incompatible-output check were both discovered only after a GPU fleet had been
paid for, and idle workers kept their machines alive to the end of the run
rather than releasing them as the campaign's do.

The honest finding from that work is a gap in coverage, not in code: moving the
single-region path's tile size *and* re-cutting its entire output geometry broke
no test. The campaign path has flow-level and end-to-end tests; that path had
none, and the assembly tests build their own small grids, so they assert whatever
geometry they are handed. A chain test now drives it at the real tile size over a
mosaic with a ragged edge, and a laptop configuration sized to actually exercise
the chunk grid is included — the shipped quickstart region is smaller than a
single chunk, so it proved the pipeline ran and nothing about its geometry.

### Orchestration

```
run the campaign
   ├─ seed the store           (one time: create the 120 zones)
   ├─ build the land mask      (one time: registry → coverage bitmaps)
   ├─ export the zone masks    (optional: pre-generate + validate all 120 up front)
   └─ for each pending (zone, year):
          ingest the inputs → fill (run the model + write results) → drop the mosaic
```

The campaign driver walks the outstanding work most-recent-year first, runs
many zones at once, and only needs a zone's inputs to exist just before that
zone runs. Already-finished or all-ocean zones are settled cheaply without ever
starting a GPU fleet. You can scope a run to specific zones, or point it at
pre-existing inputs and skip ingestion.

### Two ways to run the fills

The fills can be scheduled onto hardware in two ways:

- **A fleet per zone** (the original, default): each zone-year spins up its own
  GPU fleet, uses it, and tears it down. Simple and maximally parallel.
- **A shared fleet per group of zones** (new, opt-in): a handful of long-lived
  fleets each work through a group of the year's zones back to back, preparing
  the next zone's inputs and writing out the finished zone's results in the
  background so the GPUs stay busy at the seams. This pays the (slow, sometimes
  capacity-constrained) fleet-startup cost once per group instead of once per
  zone — hundreds of GPU-hours and a lot of capacity risk saved — at the cost of
  running a group's zones in sequence rather than all at once.

Both produce identical results; the choice is purely about cost versus
wall-clock.

### Handling missing radar — pixels, and whole regions

Some pixels have valid optical imagery but little or no radar coverage. By
default those pixels are skipped. An opt-in setting lets the campaign embed them
anyway (using the model's neutral "no radar" input), so coverage gaps don't
leave holes — with the affected pixels flagged in the output so consumers can
tell them apart. It's off by default and documented as needing a quality check
before production use.

The same problem exists a level up, and it is geography rather than a fault.
Over ice, Sentinel-1 flies a different mode whose polarisations this pipeline
deliberately discards, so those regions have **no usable radar at all** — and a
global product cannot refuse them. A zone with no radar is therefore ordinary
work: the orbit resolver may settle on "none", and the campaign carries that
per cell rather than treating it as a failed ingest to retry forever.

The opposite case is still real and is preserved as an opt-in. A single run over
terrain known to be imaged, where a missing radar store means something upstream
broke, can demand radar and fail rather than quietly embedding without it. That
switch is available on the single-region and per-cell paths and deliberately not
on the global campaign, where allowing none is always the right answer.

### When the source data itself is the problem

Two failures that only appear at scale, both now handled rather than fatal.

**The catalogue holds more than one copy of a date.** Element 84 keeps a separate
item per reprocessing of the same tile and acquisition, which is common rather
than exceptional — a single tile can have dozens of duplicated dates in a season.
The loader mosaics every item in a day's group, so two things went wrong at once:
an unreadable copy failed the whole date even though a good copy existed, and the
two copies can sit on either side of a reflectance-correction threshold, so a
fused date could hold pixels processed both ways with exactly one correction
applied — decided by item order. Duplicates are now reduced to one copy per
tile-date, newest first, before the loader sees them. Choosing up front is also
what makes a fallback possible at all: while both copies are in the group there
is nothing to fall back *to*. The older copy is used only after the newer one has
demonstrably failed to read, never as a default — sampling found duplicate copies
intact, so age is not evidence of corruption.

**Some source objects will never read.** A transient read is retried; past that,
the date steps down to its next catalogue copy, and when every copy has failed
the date is skipped and *recorded on the store*, so the loss is a finding rather
than an unexplained gap. Failures name the granule and the date, which is what
made the duplicate pattern visible in the first place.

## Getting it right, and safely

Because a mistake can be expensive (a committed year is permanent, and a GPU
fleet is billed by the minute), the design leans heavily on checking before
acting and cleaning up after itself:

- **Pre-flight gates.** Before any GPU fleet starts, a fill refuses to proceed
  if the requested window isn't the target calendar year, if the inputs don't
  cover the window, if an input grid doesn't line up with the seeded zone grid,
  or if the store was seeded for a different model version than the one running.
- **Restartable.** Each zone's in-progress work is fingerprinted by its actual
  inputs and code version, so a retry with the same inputs resumes where it left
  off, while any real change starts fresh — a stale or interrupted run can never
  quietly mix old and new results into a permanent year. The input side of that
  fingerprint is the storage system's own revision identifier for each input
  mosaic, not a bookkeeping timestamp the writer is trusted to update, so an
  input that changes by any route at all is detected.
- **Cost controls.** Many zones infer in parallel, but the contended
  store-commit step is rate-limited fleet-wide to avoid overwhelming storage,
  and the storage write budget is shared out across concurrent fills rather than
  multiplied by them.
- **One stuck worker no longer holds the fleet.** A single chunk can hang inside
  a GPU call that never returns, and the stall detector only acted when *many*
  chunks stalled together — which one never reaches. Measured on a real cell: one
  chunk hung partway through, and after every other chunk had finished the run
  held twenty GPU workers for a further seven hours, 31.6 GPU-hours on a cell
  whose real work cost a fraction of that. A single wedged chunk is now recovered
  on its own. It has to be a kill rather than a timeout: the hang is below Python,
  so nothing can interrupt the thread, and forcing past it would leave the GPU in
  an unknown state — turning a loud, local stall into quiet corruption.
- **Long-lived credentials are renewed on a clock**, not opportunistically as
  work passes through, so a fleet that spends hours on one cell doesn't expire
  mid-run; and a failed leg of a zone's input preparation is re-dispatched rather
  than leaving the mosaic permanently incomplete.
- **Clean teardown.** If a run is cancelled or crashes, its GPU fleet is torn
  down and any in-flight input-prep jobs are cancelled — reliably, even when the
  controlling process is killed before it can clean up itself — so nothing keeps
  billing or keeps writing where a retry will reuse.
- **Bounded disk.** In the shared-fleet mode, the number of multi-terabyte input
  mosaics kept on disk at once is capped, in both the everything-succeeds and
  everything-fails directions.
- **Consistent storage access.** Storage credentials and region are threaded
  through every read and write, so a store that needs an explicit region or
  credential callback is accessed the same way everywhere.

## Recovery under interruption

A campaign of this size will be interrupted, so the branch treats "what happens
on the retry" as a first-class property rather than an afterthought. Three
mechanisms, each with its own failure it was written for:

- **Resume, don't rebuild.** An interrupted mosaic is picked up where it stopped.
  Icechunk commits a date's time slot atomically with its pixels, so a date
  present is complete and a date absent was never started — there is no partial
  date to repair. The previous clear-and-rebuild discarded everything a dense
  zone had ingested for any interruption at all, and interruptions are expected
  because the orphan sweeper cancels runs by design.
- **Retry a zone, don't abandon the campaign.** A failed zone no longer sinks the
  run. Each year gets a bounded number of rounds, and every round re-reads the
  store for what is still missing, so a retry never repeats a zone that landed.
  Rounds stop early when one makes no progress — that is what a deterministic
  failure looks like from the driver, and it wants a human rather than another
  fleet. The campaign raises at the very end listing every cell it could not
  fill, so a run's failures stay visible.
- **Re-running the whole campaign is safe.** A fresh run recomputes nothing that
  already landed: completed work is filtered at the campaign work list, at the
  per-zone ingest marker, at date-level resume inside ingest, and at staged-tile
  resume inside inference. Two deliberate exceptions — a changed parameter raises
  rather than quietly mixing two configurations, and a code change invalidates
  staged tiles.
- **A half-written staged tile is re-run, not trusted.** An inference tile is
  written to staging as many objects with no atomic commit, so a crash mid-upload
  leaves one whose missing pieces read back as fill values rather than as an
  error — the shape of silent data loss the rest of this branch exists to prevent.
  A tile therefore counts as finished only if its completion marker landed. The
  marker is a sibling object visible in one listing of the staging prefix, so
  classifying a run's thousands of tiles as finished, interrupted or deliberately
  skipped costs a single request — that listing is the gate, and both assembly
  entry points now run it rather than trusting whoever called them. An interrupted
  tile is re-inferred and overwritten in place; nothing needs deleting by hand.
  A second copy of the same fact is stored inside each tile and checked by one
  shared opener at read time. It is not a parallel gate; it covers the one case a
  listing cannot, since a listing is taken once in the driver while tiles are read
  much later in worker processes, and a tile rewritten in between would otherwise
  be reported as the listing last saw it. This folds in the fix from #88, which
  found the same gap independently against `main`.

The most recent review round found the failure that defeated all of this for one
specific interruption: a run that died between its last date commit and the
record of which window it examined left a store that every subsequent retry
resumed, wrote nothing to, and therefore never repaired — so a legitimately empty
month stayed indistinguishable from a missing one and the zone-year could never
complete. That record is now keyed on the store rather than on what the current
attempt wrote. The same round tightened four other interruption paths: the create
path now refuses to overwrite a store whose contents it could not read, cluster
teardown is time-bounded so the terminate-by-tag fallback stays reachable, a
failed ingest no longer counts as a finished mosaic and so cannot start a GPU
fleet for work that does not exist, and the ingest window is started inside the
cleanup guard so no child ingest is ever orphaned.

A following round caught the same class of problem in the grid check that guards
against misgeoreferencing. Inference writes pixels by position rather than by
coordinate, so a supplied mosaic is validated against the destination zone's grid
first — but that validation compared only each axis's length, projection and two
endpoints, which a shuffled or non-affine interior satisfies. Uniform ten-metre
spacing is now asserted on both axes, which pins the axis exactly. The campaign's
own ingest cannot produce a bad one; the path that accepts a hand-staged mosaic
can, and it is supported.

A later round surfaced the sharpest of these, in a different place: the ingest
window is a range of solar days, but every catalogue query is bounded in UTC, and
the two disagree wherever a zone's solar offset crosses UTC midnight. The
month-slicing pads each query by a day so a straddling solar day is fetched whole
— but those pads were clamped to the window, so at the year's own two edges the
padding vanished and the first and last day of every zone-year were written with
part of their imagery unfetchable by any slice. Invisibly, because the recorded
assessed window still covered them and the month coverage gate still passed. The
pads are now unclamped; what excludes out-of-window dates is the solar-day
ownership filter, which is what excluded them all along.

**The radar counterpart of that has since landed**, and it was the one item
previously carried here as deferred. The radar ingest walked the year in
thirty-day chunks cut on UTC dates while the loader grouped images into solar
days, so where the two are far apart a day straddling a chunk boundary was
written from one side only and the other side discarded as a duplicate. It bit
where midnight UTC coincides with the satellite pass — UTM zones 46 and 47 in the
east, 14 and 15 in the west, and zone 47 is the third-densest zone on Earth.
Padding alone would only have moved which day was truncated, so the radar path
now has the same own-versus-query separation the optical path has: each batch
queries a padded UTC range and writes only the solar days it owns. That also
closed the related gap where radar could write a date outside the requested year.
Solar day is now the single convention everywhere, for both sensors, with the
longitude offset applied exactly once and an architecture rule that fails the
build if it is ever applied anywhere else.

Two rejections from those rounds are recorded on their threads. A reviewer asked, repeatedly,
for a configuration fingerprint to be stamped on every in-progress ingest store
so a resumed store could be checked for a settings change. Declined: anything
about the configuration that must be preserved belongs in the project manifest,
which is this repository's single point of truth, and the manifest already closes
the only component that can drift without a human editing a parameter — it
carries the land-mask hash and validates it on every single write, so a resumed

marker probe. A second reviewer asked for machinery to distinguish a zone-year
that was all ocean from one observed all year that never produced a usable pixel.
Also declined: no data is no data, whatever produced it, and the store is not
obliged to record which kind of nothing a gap represents.

The same reasoning removed one of this branch's own additions. A fail-closed
check added to the store-creation path during these rounds was dropped again once
it became clear it guarded a function the campaign never calls.

### The most recent round

A backlog of thirty-three review threads was worked to zero. Deduplicated it was
about ten findings — one of them reported ten separate times — and four could
have destroyed or silently corrupted data:

- **A failed read could have erased a finished mosaic.** The routine reporting
  which dates a store already holds swallowed every error and answered "none",
  and that answer is what routes a write between appending and creating. A
  momentary read failure therefore sent a fully populated store down the create
  path, which overwrites. It now answers "none" only for genuine absence, and the
  overwriting step re-checks the store itself rather than trusting a network read.
  Worth recording that the first version of that guard was itself destructive: the
  cleanup that removes a half-written store on failure deleted the store the guard
  had just refused to overwrite, until the refusal was given a type exempt from it.
- **The campaign could report success having skipped work.** It concluded a round
  on the child job's report instead of re-reading the store — contradicting its
  own stated rule two lines below — and a child can legitimately report success
  having never started some cells. It now re-reads every round, and the child
  reports what it never attempted.
- **The restart fingerprint missed the code that shapes the data.** It covered the
  inference package but not two modules reached through it, one of which computes
  a model input. It now follows imports transitively, because a hand-maintained
  list goes stale the first time someone adds an import, and goes stale silently.
- **The default fill strategy ignored that fingerprint entirely.** The shared-fleet
  mode computed its own identity from the machine image, so on the mode campaigns
  actually run, re-baking the image abandoned every staged tile and both documented
  controls for staging reuse did nothing at all.

## Design records and validation

The decisions behind all of this are written up as design records in the repo
(global-store architecture, the land-mask approach, and campaign ingestion),
which are the place to look for the "why" behind a given choice rather than
re-deriving it. The ingestion performance work has its own record, which keeps
the measured effect of every change alongside the ones that were tried and
abandoned — including a 23% reduction in coordination work that turned out to buy
no wall-clock time at all, which is the finding that redirected the rest of the
effort. All figures quoted above come from there, measured on the same cell so
they compare.

**The cost model is now measured rather than projected**, and the records track
the corrections as well as the conclusions. Three findings matter for planning.
Contention between simultaneous fleets prices at zero at seventeen of them, so
the ladder's remaining rungs are blocked on a quota raise rather than on any
doubt. Observations per pixel — the term that sets inference cost — are taken
directly from what the runs report rather than modelled, and come in about half
the census estimate. And measured ingest velocity sits well under the duration
basis the plan assumed; the investigation rules out six candidate causes, each
with the measurement that eliminates it, and names what is left. Several entries
are corrections of earlier entries, including one figure corrected three times
and two claims withdrawn outright, which is deliberate: the record is meant to
show what was believed and why it changed, not only what survived.

The change is covered by an extensive unit and architecture test suite — around
1,890 tests, with the pre-existing ones continuing to pass unchanged, confirming
the results are unaffected — and formatting, linting, and type checks are clean.

It was driven through more than fifty automated code-review rounds that
stress-tested the concurrent and failure paths in particular, and every thread
they raised is resolved. The fixes those surfaced — input-georeferencing
